description: We are a group of high school students. We are very dedicated to every challenge we participate in. We are also interested in a wide variety of topics, from coding to building.
summary: Our team developed Aevion, an interactive web application that uses NISAR radar data to track and visualize surface change at locations around the world. These changes are hard to see and understand, and clouds hide many of them from ordinary satellites. Aevion presents five of them as short, interactive stories on a satellite map: the Venezuela earthquakes, the Kīlauea and Krasheninnikov volcanoes, Mexico City’s sinking ground, and the July 2026 Upper Assam floods. Each story has charts, a plain-language Story mode, a Scientist mode for the numbers, and text in the local language of its place. In Assam, a slider compares the dry season with the flood peak across seven dates, rain sits beside flooded area, and users can click any spot to see if it flooded. On 22 July, near the peak, NISAR showed up to 729 square kilometers under water, and we checked our water threshold against an independent flood map from Assam University. The Assam floods are especially important to us, because friends and family of ours there were hit hard. Aevion helps people see how much the ground changed and who it affected. Aevion ensures that people with different backgrounds have an equal opportunity to access our information and data.  We included a wide variety of features that helps turn possibly confusing information into information that anyone can understand and learn from.
details:
What it does and how it works

Aevion turns NISAR radar data into short, guided stories on a satellite map. Python scripts download the NISAR products and NASA’s ARIA displacement map, crop them to each study area, and convert them into images the map can display. A React and TypeScript web app, built on MapLibre, presents the results.

For the Assam floods, we classify a pixel as water when its HH radar signal falls below -15 dB. It counts as new flood water only if it was not water in the dry-season image and is not permanent water. We checked that threshold against an independent flood map from Assam University. Rainfall comes from NASA’s GPM IMERG data, and population estimates come from WorldPop.

Benefits

Radar sees through cloud, which matters because floods are often at their worst when cloud hides the ground. Aevion explains each result in plain language, while a Scientist mode gives experts the numbers. We still ensure that anybody can understand the data and information by making sure the graphs and maps are readable with clear outlines and legends. We also provided more accommodations to benefit a larger scope of people, such as through translation. Every story includes charts and can be read in the language of its place. We label estimates honestly, and a short link reopens exactly the view you were looking at.

Intended impact

We want more people to understand what NISAR can show. In the Assam story, we want people to see how far the floods reached and who lived under the water. Adding a new story only takes a folder of data, so other teams can build their own.

Tools

Python (numpy, h5py), TypeScript, React, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, Esri World Imagery, AWS terrain tiles, Git and GitHub, and Vercel for hosting. We also used Claude Code, an AI coding assistant. We worked on laptops, with no special hardware.

What’s creative

We built stories, not a dashboard. In Assam, the before/after slider tilts when the map moves into 3D, and the timeline places rain next to flooded area. One app covers five places, each in its own language, and Assam leads because it is personal to us.

What we considered

  • Honesty: Every flooded area is an upper bound, since flooded rice paddies are counted too, and data labels such as “provisional” always stay visible.
  • Accessibility: The data colors are color-blind safe, and the slider works with a keyboard.
  • Speed: Images load one date at a time, and the swipe drags a lighter picture.
  • Translations: More languages opens the opportunities to use the information to more people.
  • Credit: We credit every data source we use.
